item.title: where does the scroll end?
item.description: infinite scrolling is an engineered wrong attractor. Social media addiction is formalized as entrapment in a design built through intentional variable-ratio reinforcement. The sources indicate that infinite scrolling is a deliberate design choice that creates difficult-to-break loops and shares clinical markers with other addictions.

item.title: Does your interaction actually stop the hate?
item.description: Current hate speech detection is reactive. Offensive messages are often only reviewed by human moderators if a user files a complaint. The sources describe the mechanisms and failures of online hate speech management rather than providing evidence that active engagement reduces hate speech.

item.title: Is your kindness a biological defense?
item.description: Social threat responses can increase your risk of disease. A multilevel biological threat response to social situations can increase risk for viral infections and inflammation-related disease conditions when sustained. The evidence shows that parental altruism is associated with lower anxiety and higher trust, but it also establishes that humans have a biological system for responding to social threats that can have physical health consequences.

item.title: Is your home's warmth costing you your health?
item.description: Household air pollution is linked to 0. This global burden of premature mortality is a consequence of household air pollution from solid fuels. The evidence is mixed regarding the specific impact of rustic wood smoke on cardiovascular risk. The evidence confirms that household air pollution from solid fuels is a major driver of global mortality and developmental issues, but it does not specifically isolate 'rustic' wood smoke from fireplaces as a primary cause of cardiovascular risk.

item.title: Does your screen change how you feel time?
item.description: Interactive media increases your perception of time. Engaging with interactive content changes how you experience the passage of hours. This finding is currently supported but not definitively proven as a universal rule. The evidence shows that interactive media can increase time perception and flow, but it does not specifically confirm that high-frequency consumption distorts neural processing speed.

item.title: Why does choosing feel so heavy?
item.description: Algorithmic personalization reduces decision efficiency when you feel manipulated. When you perceive digital personalization as a strategy to control you, the cognitive cost of choosing increases. This happens because your persuasion knowledge activates. The evidence confirms that decision fatigue is a real phenomenon driven by cognitive costs, persuasion knowledge, and perceived responsibility in digital environments.

item.title: Why is it so hard to choose your future over your present?
item.description: Your brain values consumption over effort. Present bias for real consumption is stronger than for real effort. This makes it harder to choose long-term goals over immediate rewards. The evidence confirms that temporal discounting and present bias contribute to impulsive and habitual behaviors, but it does not specifically address long-term planning for climate change.

item.title: Is your brain losing its grip on reality?
item.description: Your brain does not lose its truth-sensing hardware. Misinformation does not degrade the anterior cingulate cortex. This area remains active during dishonest decisions. Evidence on this specific degradation is currently mixed. The sources show that cognitive load and information overload facilitate the spread and persistence of misinformation, but they do not provide evidence that high-frequency exposure to misinformation degrades the brain's ability to activate the anterior cingulate cortex.

item.title: Can a machine know how you feel?
item.description: Systems can recognize your emotions from your heart and brain. Affective computing can automatically identify your emotional states by analyzing neural and cardiac dynamics. This technology is capable of recognizing and forecasting your feelings. The evidence confirms that wearable technology can be used to recognize and forecast emotions, but it also highlights significant hurdles regarding data reliability and ethical privacy implications.

item.title: Does every noise affect a child's brain?
item.description: Noise affects children differently depending on the source. Evidence links aircraft noise to lower reading performance, but some road and railway noise show no effect on attention or executive function. The evidence suggests a link between noise and cognitive performance in children, but results are inconsistent and often of low or moderate quality.

item.title: Does being nice make you less happy?
item.description: High agreeableness correlates with higher marital satisfaction. The data shows that being agreeable is linked to better relationships and positive affect, rather than lower life satisfaction. The evidence on its impact on overall well-being remains mixed. The evidence does not support the idea that high agreeableness leads to lower life satisfaction; instead, it is linked to higher marital satisfaction and positive affect.

item.title: Is your spice rack linked to biodiversity?
item.description: Biodiversity is inextricably linked with spice production. The health of an ecosystem is tied to how we produce spices. However, the evidence does not show the historical impact of maritime trade or tropical degradation. The evidence confirms that monocultures are less biodiverse than mixed-species stands and that biodiversity is linked to spice production, but it lacks specific data on historical trade impacts.

item.title: Are you actually who you think you are?
item.description: Your personality is not a fixed state. Personality traits are both stable and changeable throughout your life span. Targeted interventions can produce measurable changes in your traits. The evidence shows that personality is not fixed and can be significantly altered through targeted interventions, especially for those with specific goals.

item.title: Who is actually doing the work in your remote team?
item.description: You cede your responsibility to virtual assistants. In online experiments, people show social loafing tendencies when working with virtual assistants and tend to give up their share of the work to the technology. The evidence confirms that social loafing occurs in virtual and online environments, often correlating with larger group sizes and the delegation of responsibility to technology.

item.title: Does your smoothie actually lower your Glycemic Index?
item.description: Extracting nutrients from certain fruits can lower their Glycemic Index. While smoothies require more meals to maintain a low Glycemic Load, the process of nutrient extraction in specific fruits like raspberries and passionfruit can actually reduce their Glycemic Index. The evidence contradicts the proposed angle by showing that nutrient extraction can lower the Glycemic Index of certain fruits, even though smoothies are associated with higher meal counts to maintain a low Glycemic Load.

item.title: Is your face hiding your thoughts?
item.description: The evidence does not support this claim. Current research on emotion recognition and facial motor circuits provides no data on whether surveillance causes you to subconsciously alter your expressions. The evidence is mixed and inconclusive. The sources discuss emotion recognition technology, facial motor circuits, and medical biomarkers, but none address the psychological impact of surveillance on facial expressions.

item.title: Does your cleaning routine irritate your lungs?
item.description: Your cleaning products cause symptoms without changing your lung function. Experimental data shows that volatile organic compounds (VOCs) cause dose-related respiratory symptoms, but they do not significantly change lung function or biomarkers of airway inflammation. The evidence confirms that VOCs are associated with respiratory symptoms and asthma onset, but it also shows that these exposures do not necessarily result in measurable changes to lung function or specific inflammation biomarkers.

item.title: Who decided what your medicine does?
item.description: Commercial interests have shaped anthropology for nearly a century. Business interests have influenced the development of the field of anthropology. They also shape the types of pharmaceutical effects that are made and remade for society. The evidence confirms that commercial interests influence anthropological development and pharmaceutical production, but it lacks specific data on the funding of early biological studies for labor exploitation.

item.title: Do you like them because they are familiar?
item.description: Social associations are distinct from simple repeated exposure. Social association can modify perception and alter expectancies automatically. This is not the same as simply seeing something many times. The evidence shows that familiarity and social associations influence perception and decision-making, but they are not always synonymous with simple repeated exposure.

item.title: Does your past have more power than your present?
item.description: Your attention flows more toward the past than the present. The secondary flow of attention to past events generated by remembering processes is larger than the primary attention flow to the current event. The evidence shows that digital environments create a tension between reduced individual memory retention and increased cascading flows of attention to historical data.

item.title: Does your city's hum change your brain?
item.description: Chronic noise could induce Alzheimer’s-like changes in your brain. Research suggests noise exposure is linked to amyloid-β deposition and tau hyperphosphorylation in the hippocampus and cortex. This evidence is mixed, involving both rat experiments and human observations. The evidence suggests that chronic noise exposure is associated with cognitive decline and specific neuropathological changes, though it also impacts cardiovascular health and children's verbal performance.

item.title: Does your convenient meal have a hidden cost?
item.description: No study shows ultra-processed foods provide health benefits. Research consistently links these foods to metabolic dysfunction and systemic inflammation across all life stages. There is no evidence of any beneficial health outcomes. The evidence consistently links high ultra-processed food consumption to metabolic issues and inflammation, though many studies are observational and require further research to confirm causality.

item.title: Does your phone drain your brain when it is silent?
item.description: The mere presence of a phone reduces your cognitive capacity. Even if you do not touch the device, it occupies your mental resources. The evidence on this is mixed, however, as some larger studies find no significant effect. The evidence is mixed, with some studies showing a 'brain drain' effect on working memory and cognitive capacity while others find no statistically significant impact.

item.title: Is your sleep actually impairing your brain?
item.description: Chronic excessive sleep causes large impairments in attention. People with narcolepsy type 1 and idiopathic hypersomnia show large impairments in attention, with effect sizes of -0.90 and -0.97 respectively. The evidence shows that while chronic hypersomnolence is linked to significant cognitive deficits, strategic napping can be beneficial for performance provided it avoids the period of sleep inertia.

item.title: Who is your leader really serving?
item.description: Dark traits favor opportunistic profit over promotion. Research links dark triad traits to profit manipulation and bullying rather than direct promotion rates. The evidence on how these traits impact corporate structures is mixed. The evidence shows that dark triad traits are associated with opportunistic behaviors like profit manipulation and bullying, and can be beneficial for internationalization, but it does not directly measure promotion rates.

item.title: Does your brain actually need the hippocampus to find your way?
item.description: Your brain may not need the hippocampus to remember where you are. Evidence suggests that the hippocampus might not be required for the storage or recovery of a spatial layout experienced long before an injury. The sources do not provide evidence that modern cities atrophy the hippocampus; instead, they suggest the hippocampus might not be required for long-term spatial storage and highlight other brain structures involved in navigation.

item.title: Is your probiotic helping the wrong bacteria?
item.description: Probiotics can act as a reservoir for antibiotic resistance. The most popular probiotic, Lactobacillus, can harbor genes that protect bacteria from antibiotics. These genes can then move from the probiotic to harmful bacteria in your body. The evidence shows that Lactobacillus probiotics can harbor and transfer antibiotic resistance genes to pathogens, particularly in laboratory settings.

item.title: Does doing good make it easier to do wrong?
item.description: Good deeds can license your next selfish act. When you do something good, you may feel entitled to act poorly later. This effect is stronger when people are watching you. The evidence for this is mixed and some studies have failed to replicate it. The evidence shows that while moral licensing exists and is influenced by social observation and concrete thinking, its effects are inconsistent across different studies and replication attempts.

item.title: Does your diet change your internal biology?
item.description: Industrial diets change your microbes but not your diversity. Western diets reshape the specific types of bacteria in your gut without necessarily reducing the total variety of species present. The evidence shows that industrialization and Western diets significantly reshape the specific types of microbes present in the human gut, but it does not confirm a systematic reduction in overall microbial diversity.

item.title: Who actually decides how your city grows?
item.description: Elite capture undermines policy in several sectors. The evidence shows that elite capture influences urban planning, welfare distribution, and oral health policy, but it does not specifically address pharmaceutical profits. The sources confirm that elite capture is a recurring mechanism that undermines policy intent in various sectors like urban planning, welfare, and oral health, but they do not specifically address the pharmaceutical profit motive.

item.title: Is your screen eroding your ability to read a room?
item.description: Virtual environments can be used as therapeutic tools for social training. Technology is being used to help people implement real-time social interaction. The evidence confirms that digital communication lacks real-time non-verbal cues which can hinder emotional understanding, but it also shows that technology is being developed to simulate or facilitate these interactions.

item.title: Who knows your daily routine better than you?
item.description: Your home is no longer a private space. Smart home technology can effortlessly collect data on your presence and the time you spend on specific activities. The evidence on this is mixed regarding long-term clinical effects. The evidence shows that smart home technology enables granular behavioral tracking and prediction, though its direct impact on clinical outcomes remains unproven and user awareness is not a strong driver of security behavior.

item.title: Is your craving a choice or a physical rewiring?
item.description: Your brain physically rewires itself to favor addiction. Chronic substance use creates maladaptive neuroplasticity and brain inflammation that alter your reward and decision-making circuitry. The evidence shows that substance use causes structural and functional changes in the brain's reward and executive systems through maladaptive neuroplasticity and inflammation.

item.title: Does talking actually solve your problems?
item.description: Some people report less rumination when they talk less. Certain facets of alexithymia are linked to lower reports of rumination and social sharing. The sources do not provide evidence that talking about problems reinforces negative neural pathways; instead, they show varied emotional processing and regulation strategies.

item.title: Is your flow state just a distraction?
item.description: Flow requires simulation and skill balance. The experience is not just high arousal. It depends on a balance between your skill and the task challenge. The evidence shows that flow is a complex state involving dopaminergic function and reward structures, but it also requires specific cognitive balances and sensory-motor simulation.

item.title: Is your feed actually showing you everything?
item.description: Algorithmic systems structurally amplify ideological homogeneity. While some studies show personalization can match human editorial variety, internet customization effectively isolates individuals from diverse opinions. The evidence is mixed, with some studies confirming the existence of filter bubbles and others finding that the effects on news diversity may be exaggerated or manageable.

item.title: Is your behavior a biological trait or a social regulation?
item.description: Medicine used terms to judge womanhood. Mid-twentieth century physicians used the term sexual frigidity to judge a woman's autonomy, character, and the success of her marriage. The evidence shows that certain pathologies were constructed to enforce social norms and gender roles, but it does not provide a comprehensive history of state economic requirements.

item.title: Does low-fat dairy really cause weight gain?
item.description: Low-fat diets with high fiber and protein are supported for weight management. The evidence does not link low-fat dairy to weight gain. Instead, it supports a diet reduced in fat and sugar-rich beverages, with more fiber-rich carbohydrates and protein. The sources do not provide evidence that low-fat dairy products specifically cause weight gain; instead, they suggest that a low-fat diet with high fiber and protein is a supported strategy for weight management.

item.title: Does social rejection actually hurt like a burn?
item.description: Social rejection does not use the same pain matrix as physical injury. A statistical analysis of 244 participants failed to support the claim that social rejection operates on the same pain matrix as physical pain. The evidence suggests that social pain is more complex than a simple literal activation of the physical pain matrix, as studies failed to find a consistent overlap with nociceptive stimuli.

item.title: Can the soil keep producing forever?
item.description: The Green Revolution linked to permanent soil health degradation. The push for higher grain yields in India is linked to the loss of soil flora and fauna. It is also linked to systematic damages to the soil, groundwater, and ecosystem. The sources provide evidence that Green Revolution Technologies are linked to significant environmental and soil degradation in India and other regions.
